Introduction With the rapid adoption of generative AI, more and more enterprises need to provide AI Agent services to internal teams or external customers. How to achieve efficient, low-cost multi-tenant AI Agent deployment while ensuring security isolation has become a key technical challenge. This article describes how to build an OpenClaw AI Agent platform that supports multi-tenancy and multi-model based on Amazon EKS, AWS Graviton, and the Kubernetes Operator pattern, and enables user self-service Provisioning through a CloudFront + Cognito + ALB front-end architecture. 2. OpenClaw Overview and Value OpenClaw is an open-source cloud-native AI Agent runtime platform that can serve as a user's personal AI assistant, providing services across multiple channels such as Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, and Signal. It is not just a chatbot; it is an intelligent Agent with memory, a skills system, browser automation, and code execution capabilities. OpenClaw's core capabilities include: Multi-AI-provider support: Amazon Bedrock (Claude), OpenAI, SiliconFlow, etc. Extensible skills system: plugin-based architecture based on MCP (Model Context Protocol) Built-in security sandbox: secure code execution environment and browser automation Declarative configuration: declaratively manage Agent instances through Kubernetes CRDs Persistent storage: supports persistence of Agent memory and workspace For enterprise users, OpenClaw offers the possibility of delivering AI Agent capabilities as an internal service (Agent-as-a-Service) — each employee or team can have their own dedicated AI Agent, while the enterprise can centrally manage model access, costs, and security policies. 3. Challenges of Multi-tenant Scenarios When we try to extend OpenClaw into a platform serving multiple users, we face the following core challenges: 3.1 User and Model Diversity Different users may need access to different AI models (e.g., Claude Sonnet, Claude Opus), or even different model providers (Amazon Bedrock, SiliconFlow, etc.). The platform needs to flexibly support multi-model configurations while centrally managing model access credentials. 3.2 Security Isolation Guarantees Each AI Agent instance holds the user's personal data, conversation history, and workspace files. In a multi-tenant environment, we must ensure: Data isolation: data of different users is fully isolated and cannot be accessed by each other Network isolation: network traffic between Agent instances is strictly controlled Resource isolation: a single user cannot exhaust shared cluster resources Runtime isolation: provide VM-level isolation options to prevent container escape 3.3 Efficiency and Performance AI Agent interactions are real-time, and users expect low-latency responses. The platform needs to minimize performance overhead while ensuring isolation, and quickly create and start instances. 3.4 Scalability Design When scaling from 10 users to 1000 or even 10,000 users, the architecture needs elastic scaling capabilities rather than linearly increasing management complexity and infrastructure costs. 4. svedkx:303: The core challenge of a multi-tenant platform is security isolation. This article designs a four-layer isolation mechanism: Namespace-level isolation separates resource views of different users; NetworkPolicy controls network traffic between Pods; ResourceQuota prevents a single user from exhausting cluster resources; Pod Security Standard restricts Pod security contexts. For high-compliance scenarios such as finance and healthcare, it also offers Kata Containers + Firecracker microVM options to achieve VM-level hardware isolation (independent Guest Kernel), reducing container escape risk from "high" to "extremely low". This layered isolation design allows the platform to flexibly switch according to different users' compliance requirements, meeting general internal team needs while extending to high-security scenarios.

xznk2t:367: The core design highlight of this article is using the Kubernetes Operator pattern to abstract each user's AI Agent as an OpenClawInstance CRD (Custom Resource Definition). The Operator continuously watches CRD changes and automatically reconciles 9+ types of Kubernetes resources such as StatefulSet, Service, PVC, ConfigMap, Secret, and NetworkPolicy. The advantage of this declarative management is that operators only need to declare the desired state, and the Operator automatically handles intermediate state transitions and error recovery, greatly reducing operational complexity in multi-tenant environments. Compared with manually writing YAML or using Helm charts, the CRD pattern natively supports self-healing and eventual consistency, which is especially important for large-scale deployments (100+ users).
